name: Reporting and Communication
blurb: Metrics that matter, reports people read, and communication that protects the organization.

modules.title: Metrics and Reports
modules.blurb: Measuring security and writing findings that drive action.

topics.title: Security Metrics and KPIs
topics.description: MTTD, MTTR, trend analysis, and KPIs that prove the program is improving.
what: Security metrics quantify performance: MTTD (mean time to detect) measures how fast threats are found; MTTR (mean time to respond/recover) measures how fast they are handled. Trend analysis compares periods to show direction — are metrics improving or degrading? KPIs tie these numbers to goals, like cutting phishing triage time 20%.
Good metrics drive decisions; vanity metrics (raw alert counts) merely decorate slides.
why: Executives fund what numbers justify. Analysts who speak in trends and KPIs get budget, headcount, and attention — and exam questions constantly ask which metric answers which question.

concepts.text: Average time from compromise to detection — lower is better.
Average time to respond or recover — lower is better.
Period-over-period comparison showing direction of metrics.
Key performance indicator tied to a goal, e.g., triage time.
Raw counts snapshot volume; trends reveal improvement or decay.

topics.example: Executives ask whether phishing response improved this quarter. Raw counts (412 reports vs 388) say little; trend analysis shows median triage time fell from 47 to 31 minutes — the SOAR investment worked.

scenario.title: Are we getting better?
scenario.story: The board asks a blunt question: is the SOC improving year over year?

walkthrough.label: Observed activity
walkthrough.text: Request for program-level proof, not incident detail.

walkthrough.label: Initial hypothesis
walkthrough.text: Trends answer direction questions; counts cannot.

walkthrough.label: Evidence to collect
walkthrough.text: MTTD/MTTR by quarter, triage times, repeat-incident rates.

walkthrough.label: Analysis
walkthrough.text: Detection flat, response falling 30%, repeats down.

walkthrough.label: Decision
walkthrough.text: Genuine improvement with one flat spot to address.

walkthrough.label: Next action
walkthrough.text: Present trends with the detection-tuning plan attached.

technical.title: Metric chooser
technical.text: Match the question to the metric.

code.text:
How fast found?      -> MTTD
How fast handled?     -> MTTR
Getting better?       -> trend analysis
Goal-linked measure?  -> KPI
How much affected?    -> impact

exam: Period-over-period increase/decrease questions want trend analysis.
MTTD is detection speed; MTTR is response/recovery speed.
KPIs reveal what teams must prioritize — not individual performance.

confusions.text: Detect versus respond — different clocks, different owners.
Trends compare periods; counts snapshot one moment.
KPIs tie to goals; metrics merely measure.

keyTerms.def: Mean time to respond or recover.

mistakes: Answering direction questions with raw counts.
Treating KPIs as individual report cards.
examTips: Increasing/decreasing across periods screams trend analysis.
Detect versus respond decides MTTD versus MTTR.
topics.takeaway: Counts snapshot, trends direct: MTTD/MTTR plus trend analysis prove and steer the program.

checks.q: Execs ask if metrics rose or fell vs last period. Use?
Average time from compromise to detection is?
KPIs in an IR exercise mainly?

topics.title: Writing Security Reports
topics.description: Executive summaries, technical detail, and audience-tailored reporting that gets findings fixed.
what: Security reports translate findings into action. Executives need impact, risk, and cost in one page; technical teams need evidence, affected assets, timelines, and remediation steps. Every report states classification, scope, findings with severity, business impact, and prioritized recommendations with owners.
Good reports are short where leaders read and complete where engineers work — one document, two depths.
why: Unreported findings do not get fixed. Analysts who write clearly get patches approved, budgets released, and incidents understood — the exam tests audience awareness constantly.

concepts.text: One page: what happened, impact, what is needed.
Evidence, logs, timelines for practitioners.
Handling labels (confidential, need-to-know) protecting the report itself.
Prioritized actions with owners and deadlines.
What was and was not assessed — bounding the findings.

topics.example: After-action report for the adware incident: executives get impact plus the EDR-isolation success; IT gets the IOC list, timeline, and the proxy block to deploy. Same incident, two depths, one report.

scenario.title: The report nobody acted on
scenario.story: A 40-page vulnerability dump went to executives last quarter. Nothing got patched.

walkthrough.label: Observed activity
walkthrough.text: Thorough findings, zero remediation.

walkthrough.label: Initial hypothesis
walkthrough.text: Wrong depth for the audience.

walkthrough.label: Evidence to collect
walkthrough.text: Who read what, which findings had owners, what was funded.

walkthrough.label: Analysis
walkthrough.text: No summary, no priorities, no owners — engineers got prose, execs got noise.

walkthrough.label: Decision
walkthrough.text: Restructure by audience, not by scanner.

walkthrough.label: Next action
walkthrough.text: One-page executive summary plus ticketed technical appendix with owners.

code.text:
1. classification + distribution list
2. executive summary (impact, risk, ask)
3. scope and method
4. findings by severity (evidence each)
5. business impact
6. prioritized recommendations + owners + dates
7. appendices: logs, timelines, IOCs

exam: Different audiences need different depths — executives get impact, engineers get evidence.
After-action reports feed lessons learned and playbook fixes.
Reports need owners and deadlines or nothing happens.

confusions.text: Findings describe what is wrong; recommendations say how to fix it.
Classification controls handling; severity ranks urgency.

keyTerms.example: Impact plus funding ask up front.

keyTerms.def: Prioritized fix with owner and date.
keyTerms.example: Proxy block owned by NetOps, Friday.

mistakes: Sending raw scanner output to executives.
examTips: No owner plus date means no action.
topics.takeaway: Write for the reader: impact up front for leaders, evidence in back for engineers, owners everywhere.

topics.title: Documenting Incidents and Evidence
topics.description: Timelines, tickets, and evidence standards that make reports defensible and useful.
what: Documentation turns chaotic response into defensible record. Timelines order events with timestamps, accounts, hosts, and IPs. Tickets capture decisions and rationale in real time. Evidence handling — hashes, custody logs, access restrictions — keeps findings admissible and trustworthy.
Write as if auditors, lawyers, and next quarter's analysts will all read it — because they will.
why: Memory fades and staff rotate; the ticket and timeline become the incident. Exam questions reward whoever documents completely and compliantly.

concepts.text: Ordered event record: when, who, where, what.
Decisions plus rationale logged during response.
Hashes, custody, restricted access.
Pattern analysis across repeated incidents.
Tying actions to procedures for review.

topics.example: Recurring availability issues traced across four weeks: timestamps align with maintenance windows. The recurrence report — not another reboot — finally drives the fix.

scenario.title: The case that held together
scenario.story: A terminable policy violation must survive HR, legal, and possibly court.

walkthrough.label: Observed activity
walkthrough.text: High-stakes violation needing proof.

walkthrough.label: Initial hypothesis
walkthrough.text: Only airtight documentation survives.

walkthrough.label: Evidence to collect
walkthrough.text: Auth logs, web logs, workstation artifacts, full timeline.

walkthrough.label: Analysis
walkthrough.text: Independent sources corroborate.

walkthrough.label: Decision
walkthrough.text: Document to evidentiary standard.

walkthrough.label: Next action
walkthrough.text: De-identified notes, protected evidence, restricted access, HR handoff.

code.text:
2026-05-11 02:14:10Z | jdoe | WS-2042 (10.10.5.23)
  action: SMB lateral movement attempt -> blocked
  source: EDR + firewall logs | ticket INC-4471

exam: Timelines need dates, accounts, hosts, IPs — all four.
Recurring issues call for recurrence reports, not repeats of response.
Sensitive cases add de-identification and restriction.

confusions.text: Timelines order one incident; recurrence reports pattern many.
Tickets record live decisions; reports summarize afterward.

mistakes: Reconstructing timelines from memory weeks later.
Tickets with actions but no rationale.
topics.takeaway: Document live, timeline everything, and let recurrence reports end repeats.

checks.q: Four weeks of similar outages need?

modules.title: Communication and Compliance
modules.blurb: Stakeholders, disclosures, and the frameworks that govern security programs.

topics.title: Stakeholder and Crisis Communication
topics.description: Who gets told what, when, and by whom — from SOC escalation to press statements.
what: Communication scales with impact: analysts escalate to SOC leads with facts and timelines; managers brief executives with impact and options; comms teams handle press with approved statements; legal governs breach notifications to regulators and customers within mandated windows.
Pre-approved holding statements and named approvers — usually settled in tabletops — prevent Saturday-morning improvisation.
why: Technical response without communication fails the organization: customers learn from reporters, regulators fine the silence, and executives decide blind. Exam scenarios test approval chains and disclosure judgment.

concepts.text: Moving incidents up with context, not just alarms.
Pre-approved public placeholder while facts develop.
Legally mandated customer/regulator disclosure windows.
Single authorized voice preventing mixed messages.
Limiting sensitive details to essential parties.

topics.example: Friday-night customer-data leak: the SOC contains technically while the comms chief — named in the tabletop — issues the holding statement. Reporters get one consistent message; regulators get timely notice.

scenario.title: Saturday morning reporters
scenario.story: A leak posts overnight. By 8 AM reporters call asking about customer data.

walkthrough.label: Observed activity
walkthrough.text: Public exposure plus media pressure.

walkthrough.label: Initial hypothesis
walkthrough.text: Comms readiness decides reputational damage.

walkthrough.label: Evidence to collect
walkthrough.text: Confirmed scope, approved statement, notification obligations.

walkthrough.label: Analysis
walkthrough.text: Facts partial; obligations clock running.

walkthrough.label: Decision
walkthrough.text: Holding statement now, details as verified.

walkthrough.label: Next action
walkthrough.text: Single spokesperson, timed disclosures, log everything.

code.text:
SOC lead    <- facts, timeline, needs (analysts)
Executives  <- impact, options, costs (managers)
Press       <- holding statement (comms chief only)
Regulators  <- mandated notice (legal owned)
Customers   <- scoped notification (approved copy)

exam: Press timing decisions protect brand reputation — the comms officer's tabletop role.
Disclosures follow legal windows, not technical convenience.
One spokesperson, approved copy, logged timing.

confusions.text: Escalation seeks decisions upward; notification informs outward.
Holding buys verified time; disclosure follows facts.
Crisis comms informs accurately; spin distorts.

keyTerms.example: Issued Saturday while scope firms up.
Tier 1 to lead with timeline attached.

topics.takeaway: Decide comms before the crisis: one voice, approved words, legal clocks respected.

checks.q: Why bring the comms chief to a tabletop?

topics.title: Frameworks and Compliance Essentials
topics.description: NIST, ISO, PCI, HIPAA, SOX, GDPR: what each governs and when analysts invoke them.
what: Frameworks organize security work: NIST CSF structures functions (Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover); ISO 27001 certifies management systems; CIS gives build checklists. Regulations compel behavior: PCI DSS guards card data, HIPAA guards health data, SOX guards financial reporting, GDPR guards EU personal data with breach-notification teeth.
Analysts rarely implement these whole — they recognize which applies and what it demands (evidence of scanning, notifications, controls).
why: Compliance questions are recognition questions: match the acronym to its territory. Confusing them picks wrong evidence, wrong owners, wrong urgency.

concepts.text: Voluntary function-based framework for programs.
Certifiable management-system standard.
Contractual card-data security rules.
US health-data privacy and security law.
EU privacy with teeth; US financial-reporting integrity.

topics.example: PII breach with health records: HIPAA implications join the technical response — counsel scopes notification duties while the SOC scopes the intrusion. The framework decides the paperwork; the playbook decides the packets.

scenario.title: Which rulebook applies?
scenario.story: A retailer breach exposes names plus card numbers plus EU customer emails.

walkthrough.label: Observed activity
walkthrough.text: Multi-regime data exposure.

walkthrough.label: Initial hypothesis
walkthrough.text: Several rulebooks trigger at once.

walkthrough.label: Evidence to collect
walkthrough.text: Data types per record, jurisdictions, contracts.

walkthrough.label: Analysis
walkthrough.text: PCI for cards, GDPR for EU persons, state laws for notice.

walkthrough.label: Decision
walkthrough.text: Parallel technical plus compliance tracks.

walkthrough.label: Next action
walkthrough.text: Scope technically, notify per each regime's clock.

technical.title: Territory map
technical.text: One line each — enough for recognition.

code.text:
NIST CSF  -> organize your program (voluntary)
ISO 27001  -> certify your management system
PCI DSS    -> card data (contractual)
HIPAA      -> US health data (law)
SOX        -> financial reporting (law)
GDPR       -> EU personal data (law, 72h notice)

exam: Healthcare data means HIPAA; card data means PCI; EU persons mean GDPR.
NIST organizes, ISO certifies, CIS hardens — keep the verbs apart.
Compliance evidence (scan reports) differs from compliance itself.

confusions.text: Health data versus card data — different kingdoms.
NIST guides voluntarily; ISO certifies formally.
EU privacy versus US financial integrity.

examTips: Breach notice clocks are legal, not technical.
topics.takeaway: Match data to regime, regime to clock — then run technical and compliance tracks together.

checks.q: US clinic records exposed. Which regime?
EU customer emails breached. Watch for?

topics.title: Recommendations and Action Plans
topics.description: Turning findings into funded fixes: prioritized roadmaps, risk registers, and follow-through.
what: Findings die without plans. Recommendations rank fixes by risk reduction per effort, name owners and dates, and link to tickets. Risk registers record accepted and deferred risks with owners and revisit dates. Follow-up verifies fixes landed and controls hold — closing the loop from report to reality.
The best recommendation is specific, affordable, and scheduled; the worst is technically perfect and ownerless.
why: Security value equals findings fixed, not findings found. Exam questions reward plans with owners, dates, and verification over brilliant-but-orphaned advice.

concepts.text: Ordering by risk reduction, not scanner order.
Accountability plus deadline per item.
Ledger of accepted/deferred risks with revisit dates.
Verifying fixes actually landed.
Sequenced plan balancing risk, cost, and disruption.

topics.example: Post-assessment plan: week 1 — internet-facing criticals (Infra team); week 2 — compensating WAF for the unpatchable legacy app (AppSec); risk register holds the accepted low with a 90-day revisit. Every line has a name and a date.

scenario.title: Fifty findings, one quarter
scenario.story: Assessment drops fifty findings on a team of three with ninety days.

walkthrough.label: Observed activity
walkthrough.text: More work than hands.

walkthrough.label: Initial hypothesis
walkthrough.text: Triage by risk, not by page number.

walkthrough.label: Evidence to collect
walkthrough.text: Severity, exposure, effort estimates, freeze windows.

walkthrough.label: Analysis
walkthrough.text: Ten items carry ninety percent of the risk.

walkthrough.label: Decision
walkthrough.text: Risk-ordered roadmap plus register for the rest.

walkthrough.label: Next action
walkthrough.text: Owners, dates, tickets, and a verification pass.

code.text:
FINDING:  SMBv1 on 12 file servers (crit, internal)
FIX:      disable via GPO + validate (2 days)
OWNER:    Windows team | DUE: Jun 14
VERIFY:   rescan + spot-check
RISK IF DEFERRED: lateral movement path remains

exam: Plans need owners plus dates — advice without them is wrong.
Deferred risks belong in the register with revisit dates.
Verification closes recommendations, not good intentions.

confusions.text: Recommendations prescribe fixes; findings describe flaws.
Registers track accepted risk; queues track active work.
Follow-up verifies outcomes; rescans supply evidence.

keyTerms.def: Ledger of accepted risks with owners/dates.

mistakes: No revisit dates on deferred risk.
examTips: Owner plus date is always part of right answers.
Verification is the last step, always.
topics.takeaway: Findings become fixes through owners, dates, registers, and verification.

checks.q: A recommendation without an owner is?
